title: Is Science Being Replaced in Indian Schools?
description:
What happens when a country with a remarkable scientific heritage starts putting astrology, Vastu and other traditional claims into modern education?

India has a long and genuinely impressive history of science and mathematics. The decimal system and zero, the work of the Kerala school, Aryabhata's astronomy, Panini's grammar and the writings of Sushruta are all part of a real and important history of knowledge.

So teaching India's scientific heritage is not the problem.

The problem begins when history, tradition and science are treated as if they are the same thing.

In this documentary, we start with something that sounds almost unbelievable: a real postgraduate degree in astrology, recognised within India's higher education system. From there, we look at the wider Indian Knowledge Systems movement and how astrology, Vastu and other traditional subjects have entered university and vocational education.

Then the story takes a more troubling turn.

Around the same period, NCERT moved the periodic table from Class 10 to Class 11 and evolution from Class 10 to Class 12. The subjects were not completely removed, but for students who leave school after Class 10 or choose non-science streams, the practical result can be very different.

We then move into medical education, where the question becomes much more serious. What happens when ideas that might be worth studying as history become part of the education of people who will eventually treat patients?

The documentary also looks at the famous claim that Pythagoras copied his theorem from India, the real history behind the Baudhayana Sulbasutra, and why the story of independent mathematical discovery is actually more interesting than a simple "India invented it, Greece stole it" narrative.

And finally, we look at something that is often missing from conversations about Indian Knowledge Systems: India's own tradition of scepticism, including the Charvaka or Lokayata school.

Because India did not only produce traditions of faith. It also produced traditions of doubt.

The question isn't whether India should teach its intellectual heritage.

It should.

The question is whether we can teach that heritage honestly, while keeping a clear line between history and science, belief and evidence, mythology and fact.

If you want to understand how these ideas have moved beyond classrooms and into Indian politics and public life, watch my earlier documentary:

The Most Pseudoscientific Government in the World - https://youtu.be/1TZ3SHxZtJE

And if you enjoy evidence-based documentaries about science, pseudoscience, education, religion and critical thinking, subscribe to Pale Blue Thoughts.

Thank you for supporting independent science communication.

Is a master's degree in Astrology in India scientifically valid? We examine the current academic landscape and critical debates surrounding this curriculum.

This video analyzes the introduction of the new Astrology degree India curriculum, questioning its scientific validity compared to traditional academic standards. We look at the Indian Medical Association stance on the proposed MBBS BAMS integration to understand how professional bodies are responding to curriculum changes in higher education. 

By comparing these developments to the logic of Charvaka philosophy, we explore the broader implications of these policies on public discourse. We also address historical claims regarding whether Pythagoras theorem India origins are accurate or simply misconceptions. This breakdown provides clarity on how these diverse topics intersect within the current Indian education system.

transcript: In 2021, a public university in India began offering a two-year master's degree. Students would attend classes, submit assignments, sit and write examinations, and graduate with a postgraduate qualification recognized by the University Grants Commission funded in part by the state. The subject was astrology. A real master's degree that teaches students how to predict the future from the position of the planets. And it was approved by the same body that approves degrees in physics, medicine, and engineering. [music] How can the same country that sent a spacecraft into Mars orbit on its very first attempt also fund a master's degree in predicting your future from your birth chart? But an astrology degree at a university isn't where the story ends. It is where it begins. Because once an idea becomes part of a university curriculum, it gains something most beliefs never have. It gains official approval. And that is where the real story begins. Before we go any further, we need to be fair. The basic idea behind [music] Indian knowledge systems isn't ridiculous. In fact, much of it is true. India gave the world the decimal number system and the concept of zero, not just as a symbol but as a number you could actually calculate with. Centuries before Newton and Leibniz developed calculus in Europe, mathematicians from the Kerala school were already working with mathematical ideas that later became part of calculus. In the 5th century, Aryabhata calculated the length of a year with remarkable accuracy using nothing more than careful observations >> [music] >> and mathematics. These aren't exaggerated nationalist claims. They're well-documented parts of the history of science and if anything, they deserve to be taught more widely. So, the idea of teaching India's scientific heritage is not the problem. In fact, it is a good idea. The problem is what happens next. Once that idea enters the curriculum, nobody stops to ask an important question. Is this history or is it pseudo-science? The problem was that nobody seems to have checked what was being added in the name of heritage. Let us go back to the master's degree in astrology for a moment. When it was launched in 2021, it wasn't introduced as a course on the history of astrology or its place in Indian culture. It was launched as part of India's national education policy and its push to promote Indian knowledge systems. Around the same time, something similar was happening in Madhya Pradesh. The state's higher education department introduced courses in Vedic rituals, astrology, Vedic science and Vastu shastra. Students were being trained in them as professional skills. Now, I don't think I need to convince most of you that astrology and Vastu doesn't work. Decades of scientific testing have already settled that question. So, think about what that means. By 2021, public money, that is mine and yours, was being used to teach and award degrees in a subject that science had already rejected. And all this was happening while the same education system was struggling to teach millions of children basic reading and maths. And if you think that is the worst of it, it is not even close. The next example changes the stakes completely. Around the same time, something else was happening. While astrology and Vastu were finding their way into new courses, NCERT was removing some of the most important topics from the class 10 science syllabus. The periodic table was moved to class 11. Evolution was moved to class 12. Now, to be fair, NCERT didn't completely remove these topics. It said the changes were made to reduce overlap and ease the academic load after COVID. Technically, that is true. The periodic table is still taught in class 11 and evolution is still taught in class 12. But, here is the problem. Most Indian students never study class 11 science. Many leave school after class 10. Others choose streams where these topics are never taught. So, for millions of students, moving these chapters to higher classes had the same effect as removing them altogether. That is why more than 1,800 scientists and educators, including many from IITs, IISc, and IISERs, signed an open letter opposing the removal of evolution from class 10. Now, put these two facts side by side. At the same time that astrology was entering university classrooms, evolution, one of the most important ideas in all of biology, and the periodic table, a fundamental concept in chemistry, were disappearing from the last science class that many Indian students would ever attend. Pseudo science came in through the front door. Real science quietly walked out through the back. Now, imagine sitting across from a doctor. Most of us never stop to think about how they were trained because we simply assumed that everything they learned was tested against the best scientific evidence available. In 2023, the National Commission for Indian system of medicine, the body responsible for setting the curriculum for Ayurveda colleges across India added an astrology module to the Ayurveda syllabus. Now, think about what that really means. This wasn't a history department discussing ancient ideas or cultural traditions. This was [laughter] the curriculum used to train future healthcare practitioners, people who would go on to diagnose illnesses, prescribe treatments, and in some states even prescribe modern medicines. Astrology had become part of that education. The Breakthrough Science Society opposed the move, but their objection wasn't really about astrology alone. It was about where we choose to draw the line. Teaching Sushruta surgical writings as part of the history of medicine is perfectly legitimate. Teaching future health practitioners that astrology has a role in diagnosis is something entirely different, because eventually those ideas don't remain inside a classroom. They become part of how real patients are treated. The story doesn't end there. Around the same time, the University Grants Commission recommended that MBBS students should also take credit courses covering Ayurveda, Yoga, Unani, Siddha, and Homeopathy. Here, too, the important distinction is easy to miss. There is nothing wrong with medical students learning about these systems, their history, or even examining their claims scientifically. In fact, they should. But, teaching a system as evidence-based medicine is a very different claim from teaching it as the history of medicine, and that is where the debate begins. Indian Medical Association opposed the recommendation for much the same reason. Although they approached the issue from a different direction, they were ultimately making the same argument as the Breakthrough Science Society. Our medical history deserves to be he honestly, but clinical practice must be guided by evidence. As I make this video, thousands of resident doctors across Maharashtra are on a strike over a bridge course that allows homeopathy practitioners to prescribe modern medicines. Supporters argue that it helps address shortages of health care professionals. The doctors organizations argue that prescribing modern medicine requires the same scientific training and standards expected of every other doctor. Now, if homeopathy is as effective and scientific as they claim, why would they require to prescribe modern medicines? Now, whichever side you agree with, the bigger question remains the same. Where do we draw the line between studying traditional medicine and teaching doctors to use it on their patients? At the 2015 Indian Science Congress, a government minister claimed that Pythagoras hadn't really discovered the theorem named after him. According to him, it had been known in India centuries earlier, and Pythagoras had simply copied it. Now, that claim isn't supported by the evidence, but it is interesting because, like many exaggerated claims, it begins with something that is actually true. The Baudhayana Sulbasutra, a Sanskrit text on geometry written around 800 BCE, does describe the same mathematical relationship that we now call the Pythagorean theorem. That text is several centuries older than Pythagoras himself. It's a genuine historical text and an important part of India's mathematical heritage. Where the story changes is in the claim that Greece somehow stole this knowledge from India. Historians don't think that is what happened. The same mathematical relationship appears to have been discovered independently in several ancient civilizations, including Babylon, India, and Greece, because it naturally emerges once people begin studying geometry in a systematic way. And if you ask me, that is an even better story. It means India's contribution to mathematics stands on its own. It doesn't need a story about somebody else stealing it in order to be remarkable. Our myths and epics are an important part of India's cultural heritage. They deserve to be studied seriously as literature, philosophy, and religion, but they cannot, by themselves, serve as evidence that a particular scientific discovery or medical technique really existed. A story can tell us what people believed. It can tell us how they understood the world around them. What it cannot do is replace archaeological evidence, historical records, or scientific investigation. Those questions have to be answered using the methods of history and science, not the language of mythology. And this is where I think we often go wrong. Presenting mythology as science doesn't make our tradition stronger. It only puts India's real scientific achievements next to claims that have no evidence.
